---
title: "Statistical vs. Practical Significance Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Statistical vs. Practical Significance activity. Many patterns (t-tests, Cohen's d, `case_when()`) are covered in other explainers. This focuses on what is new.

## Generating large simulated datasets

```
set.seed(202)
n_users <- 5000

app_data <- tibble(
  group = c(rep("Control", n_users), rep("App Users", n_users)),
  screen_time = c(
    rnorm(n_users, mean = 240, sd = 45),
    rnorm(n_users, mean = 237, sd = 45)
  )
)
```

This creates 10,000 rows — 5,000 control users and 5,000 app users. The means differ by only 3 minutes (240 vs. 237). With such a large sample, even this tiny difference can be statistically significant, which is the point of the exercise.

## A function that returns a category

```
analyze_result <- function(p_value, cohens_d, practical_threshold = 0.3) {
  sig <- p_value < 0.05
  meaningful <- abs(cohens_d) >= practical_threshold

  category <- case_when(
    sig & meaningful ~ "Report: Both significant and meaningful",
    sig & !meaningful ~ "Caution: Significant but trivial effect",
    !sig & meaningful ~ "Investigate: Might need larger sample",
    TRUE ~ "No story: Neither significant nor meaningful"
  )

  return(category)
}
```

This function takes a p-value and an effect size and decides which of four categories the result falls into. `practical_threshold = 0.3` is a default — you can override it when calling the function. The `&` operator means AND (both conditions must be true). `!` means NOT.

## Building a quadrant chart with `annotate()`

```
annotate("rect", xmin = 0.2, xmax = 1.5, ymin = 1.3, ymax = 4,
         fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.2)
```

`annotate("rect", ...)` draws a colored rectangle on the chart at fixed coordinates. Multiple `annotate()` calls create the four colored quadrants. `alpha = 0.2` makes them mostly transparent so the data points show through. This is different from `geom_rect()`, which draws rectangles from data — `annotate()` is for fixed, manually-placed elements.

## Plotting on a transformed y-axis

```
ggplot(quadrant_data, aes(x = cohens_d, y = -log10(p_value)))
```

`-log10(p_value)` transforms the y-axis so that smaller p-values appear higher on the chart. A p-value of 0.001 becomes 3, a p-value of 0.01 becomes 2, and a p-value of 0.05 becomes about 1.3. This makes the chart easier to read because significant results are at the top.

## Building a table manually with `tibble()`

```
checklist <- tibble(
  Question = c(
    "1. What is the p-value?",
    "2. What is the effect size (Cohen's d)?",
    ...
  ),
  Why_It_Matters = c(
    "Determines statistical significance (< 0.05 threshold)",
    "Determines if the effect is large enough to matter",
    ...
  )
)

knitr::kable(checklist, caption = "A Journalist's Statistical Checklist")
```

You can build any table by hand with `tibble()` — just provide matching vectors for each column. `knitr::kable()` formats it as a clean table with an optional caption. This is useful for reference tables, checklists, or summaries that are not calculated from data.

## Common mistakes

**Confusing `&` with `|` in logical conditions:**

```
# & means AND — both must be true:
sig & meaningful    # TRUE only if BOTH are true

# | means OR — at least one must be true:
sig | meaningful    # TRUE if EITHER is true
```

Use `&` when you need both conditions to hold. Use `|` when either condition is sufficient. In `case_when()`, be especially careful — using `|` when you mean `&` will put rows in the wrong category.

**Vectors of different lengths in `tibble()`:**

```
# Error — columns must have the same number of elements:
tibble(
  Name = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Value = c(1, 2)
)

# Correct — all columns match in length:
tibble(
  Name = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Value = c(1, 2, 3)
)
```

Every column in a `tibble()` must have the same number of elements. If you get a "tibble columns must have compatible sizes" error, count your `c()` elements.
